title: The Wrong Sheet
part: PART FOUR: THE NIGHT OF THE NORTH WIND

pages.text:
*The Owl Alley Sheet, No. 18. Today's news: the wrong sheet reached the street first.*

"The fire started at the tofu shop!" Bunta’s voice boomed, shaking the frost off the eaves. "Sources say it began with the tofu maker’s careless brazier! The heat escaped, the wood caught, and the whole street is in ruins!"

Haru’s stomach dropped into her sandals. The wet ink on the sheet gleamed in the weak morning light. Bunta was not smiling. His face, hidden by the brim of his straw hat, was tight and serious. He looked down the alley, past Haru, toward the row of wooden houses. He had seen who was standing in front of him. He had seen the empty lot where Umekichi’s shop had been.

The voice slowed. It did not crackle with excitement. It was flat, heavy, and final.

"Listen to the words," Bunta said, tapping the paper with his fan. "The Turtle House knows the truth. The Turtle House always knows."

Haru felt the cold bite through her sleeves. The air smelled of wet ash and burnt timber, a sharp, acrid tang that stuck to the back of her throat. She looked at the crowd gathering behind the seller. They were quiet. They were listening. And they were looking exactly where Bunta wanted them to look.
pages.image: Bunta, a round seller in an indigo-and-white striped kimono and deep straw hat, stands in a frosty alley reading from a wet sheet, while Haru in a rust-orange kimono and indigo apron watches with wide eyes, an empty lot visible in the background.

pages.text:
The crowd turned. Slowly, like a single wave breaking against the shore, their faces shifted toward the end of the alley. Umekichi stood there, his white apron still on, his huge forearms hanging at his sides. He had not slept. He had been helping pull the shop down, and now he stood in the ash, waiting for help to build it back up.

A woman in a grey kimono stepped back. Her hand went to her mouth. A man muttered something low to his neighbor. No one shouted. No one threw a stone. That was the worst of it. It was a quiet, collective turning away.

Osen, small and quick in her dark green kimono, reached out and grabbed Umekichi’s sleeve. Her fingers were trembling. Umekichi looked at her, then at the crowd, then at the empty space where his life’s work had been. He stood as if someone had struck him with a heavy mallet, rigid and stunned. The silence in the alley was louder than any bell.
pages.image: Umekichi, a big cheerful man in a white apron and headband, stands stunned in the ash-covered alley, while Osen, small in a dark green kimono, holds his trembling sleeve, and a quiet crowd looks away in the cold morning.

pages.text:
Haru knew exactly who was wrong. She knew the wind. She knew the cracked chimney cap. She knew the tired boy who must have left the ash door ajar. But looking around the alley, she saw that nobody else knew what she knew. They only had Bunta’s loud voice and a fresh sheet of paper.

She walked quickly. Her straw sandals slapped against the wet road, a sharp, rhythmic sound in the quiet street. She crossed the alley to the Turtle House, where the glossy door curtain hung still.

Jiro was sitting on the step. He had not changed his yellow silk kimono, but it looked tired, creased and dull. In his lap sat a stack of unsold sheets. He did not look up when Haru approached. He looked at the paper in his lap, and then at her, his eyes red-rimmed and wide.

"Your father wrote this," Haru said. It was not a question.

Jiro nodded. He picked up one sheet and held it out to her. "He wrote it in the night," he said, his voice rough. "From what people said in the crowd. I told him it was not confirmed. I told him to wait."
pages.image: Jiro, a boy in a bright yellow silk kimono with a black diamond pattern, sits on the step of a wooden shop holding a stack of papers, looking exhausted, while Haru in her rust-orange kimono stands before him.

pages.text:
Jiro said no more. He looked down at his hands, which were clean and pale, a sharp contrast to the black smudges staining Haru’s fingers. He looked small, and he looked ashamed, really and truly ashamed.

It startled her. She had expected anger, or pride, or a sneer, but not this quiet, heavy shame that seemed to sit on his shoulders like a wet wool blanket.

Haru took the stack from him. She did not take just the top sheet; she took the whole pile, holding the thin paper against her hip.

"Help me print the truth," she said.

Jiro swallowed, his throat moving once. "My father will never allow it," he said softly. "He sells excitement. He will not sell a correction. He will not sell a lie that was almost true."

Haru looked at him for a moment, then reached out and placed the stack of papers back into his lap with a soft rustle. She did not ask for permission, and she did not ask for his father’s name, because she knew it would not matter.

"I am not asking your father," Haru said.
pages.image: Haru in her rust-orange kimono and indigo apron places a stack of papers into Jiro’s lap, who looks down with a shy, guilty expression, his yellow silk kimono contrasting with the grey morning light.

pages.text:
Haru walked home through the ash. The air was still cold, but the wind had died down, leaving only the faint scent of smoke. She stepped into the shop, her breath coming fast.

Father Sota was at the low table. He looked up, his face calm. He took the booklet from her belt. He did not look at her. He read the pages, from the first entry about the noodle rumor to the last line about the wind. He read slowly, his lips moving slightly.

When he finished, he closed the booklet. He looked at Haru.

"Is that everything?" he asked.

Haru nodded. "Yes. The wind. The chimney. The door."

Father Sota leaned back. He rubbed the back of his neck, a small, unconscious gesture.

"Is that the whole truth?" he asked.

Haru stopped. Her hand went to her throat. She thought of Shin. She thought of the soot on his arms, and the yawn he had tried to hide, and the fact that he was only nine years old. The truth was there, in the booklet. But the whole truth was in the boy’s eyes.
pages.image: Father Sota, a broad calm man with a white headband, sits at a low table holding a small booklet, looking intently at Haru, who stands before him in her rust-orange kimono, her expression serious and thoughtful.
